We develop a quantum relational Hoare logic that enables us to write and verify programs with multiple outputs, as well as programs that take their specification as input. Our approach is based on a probabilistic relational Hoare logic that we extend with quantum features, and we outline how we can measure the connection between inputs and outputs of programs using relational triples. At its core, the postcondition in a relational triple needs to be capable of transforming from the precondition, which is what we aim to prove. We demonstrate the efficacy of our methodology by verifying several examples, including a quantum algorithm that finds the closest pair in an unordered set of n points, even when the set is part of the input, as well as a algorithm that generates unordered pairs from an unordered set of points, even when the set is part of the input.

Determining the structure of magnetic fields on the Sun is a challenge in imaging techniques like helioseismology and observation data. A key aspect of this structure is the distinction between magnetic and non-magnetic areas, particularly their compact, strongly inclined features. Since vector magnetic field maps are prone to errors and omission, particularly in fill fractions, a new approach has been developed to accurately define this structure. This approach differentiates between magnetic and non-magnetic areas based on plausible, physically constrained models of vector fields, rather than their absolute values, which are susceptible to errors. This new method demonstrates its capability in correcting omitted areas and defining the structure of magnetic fields through a case study of a sunspot. It also shows its effectiveness in determining the true configuration of compact, strongly inclined features by comparing with existing methods.

In the context of Coxeter groups, we investigate how the number of spheres in a "wedge" is related to the size of a generating set. A key component of this research involves defining a new kind of interval that encompasses both the wedge and the prefix closure. We introduce the concept of an extended prefix interval and derive a formula that calculates its length based on the generating set and a given word. Furthermore, we define a new kind of ball that encompasses both a sphere and a wedge, and derive a formula that calculates the length of this extended ball based on the generating set and a given word.

This study delves into the concept of Bertrand curves and extends the theorem proving that a curve in certain spaces that admits a second-order differential geometry structure and is equipped with an inner product, will have a normal development with respect to curvature and hence is a rational curve.

This research develops two novel loss functions called ExpD and ExpS, which are based on the exponential divergence formula, differing only in how they handle class imbalances. ExpD and ExpS are under-represented in the literature compared to KL Divergence, which is widely used, but may offer performance gains in specific situations. To support the proposed loss functions, we also design ExpD-based and ExpS-based neural neural network classifiers that are free from regularization. To evaluate the loss functions, we conducted five deep learning experiments using ExpD-based and ExpS-based classifiers and multiple already-existing classifiers. The results showed that ExpD and ExpS generally deliver better accuracy compared to KL Divergence in many cases, and ExpD-based classifiers often produce the best outcomes.

Neural models for relation extraction have been successful but face challenges when categorizing diverse relation types due to their similar patterns and contexts. Our approach addresses this challenge by introducing a new training method that organizes relation types in a hierarchical structure, then uses neural models to learn distinctions between them. Our hypothesis is that certain relations share underlying connections and that a structure-based classification system can effectively identify relations through their unique patterns. In our experimental setup, we selected 29 relation types from the TACRED dataset to analyze their characteristics and hierarchy. Our best-performing model achieved an average precision of 71.3% across all relations and a maximum precision of 92.5% for hypernymic relations. Our findings offer a new perspective on relation types and their classification.

Our proposed technique involves a novel reformulation of the spatial attention mechanism in convolutional neural networks, leading to a more precise model of novel view video prediction. This reformulation involves a change from the traditional convolution operation to a linear transformation when constructing the auxiliary network, resulting in a more accurate description of novel views. Furthermore, we introduce a new regularization term to enhance the auxiliary network's effectiveness in novel view video generation. Our model achieves the best results in novel view video prediction compared to existing methods, based on experimental data collected from various datasets.

We provide a comprehensive investigation of how truncating the geodesic distance in a graph affects its metric dimension, as well as its smallest cardinality sub-set that distinguishes between any two vertices uniquely. It is established that for any positive integer $t$, a graph $G$ has an $\tau_t(G)$-dimension of at most $s$, where $s$ is the minimum size of a subset of vertices that can be distinguished by all integers less than or equal to $d_{max}+t$. Additionally, the same upper bound applies to the smallest sub-set of this description that distinguishes between any two vertices uniquely. It is also shown that for any positive integer $t$, an extension of a graph $H$ results in an $\tau_t($extension of $H)$-dimension of at most $s$, as well as the smallest sub-set of this description that distinguishes between any two vertices uniquely.

Our proposed method addresses the challenges of detecting cardiac abnormalities from non-invasive signals that are prone to noise and interference. Unlike existing methods that rely on precise electrode contact information, our approach uses spatial information from a sensor grid to pinpoint problematic contacts. We introduce the Novel Contact Identifier (NCI), a deep learning-based algorithm that accurately detects abnormal heart signals and eliminates noisy data. In a comprehensive evaluation involving nine individuals and multiple sensor configurations, our NCI consistently outperformed existing contact validation techniques, resulting in higher accuracy and discovering previously unknown noisy contacts. Furthermore, we incorporate the NCI into a real-time abnormal heart signal detection system that can be used for a variety of applications, including using wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) sensors to monitor cardiac health.

A research study has observed ultra-violet (UV) fine structure lines in three extreme starburst galaxies, MrK ain-3, SMM J02399-0136, and HFL96. These galaxies exhibit unusually high specific star formation rates and show signs of low-density molecular wind or circumgalactic gas reservoirs. The presence of these winds/reservoirs is indicated by the line ratios of CI fine structure lines and the [CII] line. In the case of MrK ain-3, a high CI(2577)/[CII] line ratio is observed, indicating a low electron temperature or dense gas. However, in SMM J02399-0136, a low CI(3707)/CI(2577) line ratio is found, suggesting a low density molecular wind. The line ratio of [NII] 122μm to [CII] 158μm is also high in SMM J02399-0136, pointing to the influence of a low-density molecular wind on this ratio as well. The same research study examined the relationship between CI fine structure lines and massive starbursts in the most distant quasi-starburst galaxy, SMM J16357-2408.3, which exhibits a normal CI line ratio but an abnormally low [NII] 122μm to [CII] 158μm line ratio, indicating the presence of a low-density molecular wind.

We have established explicit formulae for the velocity distribution of a second-class particle in ASEP and NEASEP at all points in time.  These schemes represent genuine ASEP and NEASEP, and also include both ASEP and NEASEP within the framework of an integrable probability lattice gas system called TASEP with collisions.  A straightforward modification of the method enables us to obtain the steady-state probability distribution of the second-class particle in TASEP with collisions.  The method based on Bethe roots can be viewed as an alternative approach to solving ASEP through the TASEP with collisions and through the RSK algorithm.  The formula derived through the first approach is more efficient, especially in calculating the asymptotic behavior of the second-class particle's velocity distribution in ASEP and NEASEP.  The asymptotic behavior in ASEP and NEASEP can also be characterized by the formula derived through the second approach.  The steady-state probability distribution of the second-class particle in ASEP and NEASEP under the half-space condition can be determined by combining the formula obtained through the first approach with the reflection principle.  The asymptotic behavior of the second-class particle's velocity distribution in ASEP and NEASEP converges to the same probability distribution as the distance from the second-class particle increases.  The average position of the second-class particle in ASEP and NEASEP can be calculated by multiplying the asymptotic velocity distribution by the integer values representing positions, and

In the context of epidemiological studies, interpreting the effects of risk factors is crucial, and this is especially true when employing differential equations to model disease dynamics.  Since parameter estimation involves fitting models to limited data, there is a risk of generating negative populations when drawing marginal distributions of certain variables.  This paper addresses this issue by developing a framework that incorporates biological constraints into differential equation models.  This framework enables the application of established Bayesian inference methods to estimate parameters that account for negative populations.  Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach on two real-world epidemiological datasets.  One dataset involves the modeling of measles dynamics, and the other involves the analysis of risk factors associated with tuberculosis transmission.  This research is significant as it provides a practical solution for incorporating biological feasibility into differential equation models, thereby enabling the exploration of underlying causes of disease spread and the identification of factors that contribute to it.

Using a massive galaxy dataset of 20,000 objects, we examined the evolution of galaxy colors by analyzing the NUV-r color distribution across various stellar masses. Notably, we discovered that, beyond a certain mass point (approximately 10^11 M solar), more substantial, less active galaxies with NUV-r > 5.0 colors begin to dominate the population. Furthermore, we found that the most common NUV-r color among massive galaxies is 4.5 < NUV-r <= 5.0, in contrast to lower mass galaxies that prefer NUV-r <= 4.5 colors. Additionally, we observed that the NUV-r color at the median point of the distribution for massive galaxies remains steady with redshift, whereas less active galaxies with NUV-r > 5.0 colors become more prevalent as lookback time increases.

Multilingual models that learn several languages simultaneously have experienced remarkable success in classification tasks. However, inducing English sentiment knowledge in such models, particularly when they are initially trained on non-English data, is found to be challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced when the models are trained on data with ambiguous sentiment labels. This research fills this knowledge gap and presents a novel regularized multi-task learning approach to train models that can classify English sentiment in conjunction with other languages. The approach focuses on optimizing the model's output over multiple languages to accurately predict sentiment. Furthermore, we develop a new dataset, consisting of multiple languages with accurately labeled sentiment, to evaluate the effectiveness of our method. The results obtained when testing the method on three languages (French, Italian, and Spanish) are impressive, demonstrating that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art in all three languages.

We report on the detection of a peculiar rotation profile in KIC 9267654, a young A-type primary star in a binary system.  This discovery was made possible by spectroscopic observations obtained over a seven year period, allowing for the mapping of the stellar rotation profile as it changes and shifts due to the differential rotation and shear induced by the shear interface between the fast and slow rotating regions of the star.  A unique feature of this star is the presence of a strong shear interface near the equator, which leads to a rotation period of 15 days in the polar regions and a period of only 12 hours near the equator.  This unusual profile is unlikely to be explained by standard mixing processes such as shear induced mixing or turbulent mixing.  However, a possible explanation is the presence of an additional mixing process driven by the shear interface itself, which could be facilitated by the strong shear seen in this particular star.  If confirmed, this discovery would indicate that turbulent mixing is not the primary process responsible for distributing angular momentum in rapidly rotating stars, and a new form of mixing could be a major driver of angular momentum redistribution in these stars.  This discovery also raises the possibility that magnetic fields could be responsible for this new form of mixing, which would be a significant finding given the potential for fields to influence rotation profiles and the formation of chemical spots.  Further observations and modeling are necessary to fully understand the nature of this phenomenon and its place within the context of ApB stars.

Fake news on social media has become a pressing concern, and automated systems are being developed to help moderate it. Our proposed MetaFEND system addresses this issue by using a deep learning-based approach to detect false information. Initially, we used a standard convolutional neural network to classify news articles, but this method yielded disappointing results. To improve the system's effectiveness, we employed a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks, which allowed us to utilize the embedding generated by a pre-trained language model to input information into the network. This customized design significantly enhanced the detection capabilities of MetaFEND, which was fine-tuned on a large dataset of true and false news articles. Our experiments using the RealNews dataset showed that MetaFEND consistently outperformed the standard CNN approach, achieving the best results when we utilized the BERT base model and allowed the system to evaluate multiple options before selecting the best outcome.

A Golay complementary array pair with respect to a metric space is a pair of complete graphs where the off-diagonal entries represent distances in the space. For a quaternary GCA pair, we present construction methods for dimensions 4r+1 and 4r+2, along with specific instances for (25, 429) and (31, 930) arrays.

Deep learning algorithms, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been highly effective in analyzing medical image data, enabling accurate segmentation of regions of interest through training on large datasets of annotated images. However, creating such datasets is a time-consuming and costly process, and it is not currently possible to manually label the vast amounts of data generated by medical imaging techniques like MRI scans. To address this challenge, a novel adaptive training strategy has been developed, which allows a pre-trained CNN to segment new, previously unseen images with minimal additional training on a small number of annotated samples. This approach has been tested on two different types of medical images: coronary artery calcification scans and brain tumor images. The results show that this method can achieve comparable segmentation accuracy compared to training the network from scratch on the full dataset, opening up opportunities to apply CNNs to a wide range of medical imaging applications with limited annotated data.

This paper introduces NeRF-X, a novel framework that seamlessly integrates classical computer vision models with neural radiance fields, enabling both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction. NeRF-X consists of a convolutional neural network, a shape encoder, a color encoder, and a rendering module, and is trained using a combination of adversarial and perceptual losses. In an unsupervised setting, NeRF-X learns from raw images, whereas a supervised setting uses labeled data. Evaluations using MNIST and SVHN demonstrate NeRF-X's effectiveness, and compared to existing methods, NeRF-X achieves better performance with simpler models and provides a more straightforward design.

Recent developments in AI research have led to the creation of large knowledge graphs, which have driven the design of a new type of transformer model, dubbed K-T5, that is pre-trained on factual triples from these graphs. Our research finds that these K-T5 models consistently outperform their text-based T5 counterparts in various question-answering tasks, according to our conducted experiments on three distinct knowledge graphs: Wikidata, YAGO, and ConceptNet. Notably, we observe that the models pre-trained on the largest available knowledge graph, Wikidata, demonstrate the most significant improvements, which amounts to an almost 100% boost in accuracy over the standard T5 model in certain cases. Furthermore, our findings indicate that K-T5 models excel particularly in question-answering tasks focused on specific domains, which suggests that they possess strong domain-adaptive learning capabilities.

In the context of non-linear Yang-Mills theories and specific models like SKP and power-law, we examine the impact of a new non-linear charge term on black hole physics, particularly for electric and magnetic monopoles. This non-linear charge term leads to a modification in the Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole metric, resulting in a distinct shadow radius. Furthermore, by introducing a heat kernel regulator to define the action explicitly, we investigate the effects on thermal profiles and shadow sizes for both electric and magnetic monopoles. Additionally, we calculate the shadow radius's polynomial expansion in a power-law model, up to the fourth order, to analyze its nonlinear charge effects.

We undertook an in-depth examination of the entanglement phenomenon in a system of two particles with the help of optical tomography. Initially, we established clear conditions under which non-classical behavior, including entanglement, can be directly observed in marginal distributions. Furthermore, we developed a straightforward method to determine the amount of entanglement (through the entanglement monotone $D_2$) based on the reduced density matrices obtained from optical tomography. To apply this methodology, we conducted a detailed analysis of a celebrated model involving two harmonic oscillators with exponentially soft-core interactions, and demonstrated how it meets the necessary criteria.

This paper discusses the extraction of branching fractions for specific decay modes of the B meson, based on experimental data from the LHCb experiment. A technique called isospin rotation is employed, where the relationship between branching fractions of different decay modes is utilized. Since the total branching fraction of the B meson to various final states must equal 1, any uncertainty associated with the branching fraction of one isospin state will directly impact the branching fraction of another isospin state. However, the approach relies on accurate calculations of radiative corrections to determine the isospin state of a given decay mode. A program called HOLLERITH is used to perform these calculations. The branching fractions of certain decay modes, including $B^0_s\rightarrow K^0\Sigma^0$, $B^0_s\rightarrow \pi^0\bar{K}^0$, $B^0_s\rightarrow \eta\bar{K}^0$, and $B^0_s\rightarrow \pi^0\pi^0$, can be determined using this method. The branching fractions of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^0\Sigma^0$ and $B^0_s\rightarrow \pi^0\bar{K}^0$ are found to be $3.9^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\times10^{-4}$ and $5.2^{+0.9}_{-0.7}\

We provide a comprehensive characterization of modules over a ring that have a straightforward, closed-form description of their submodule lattices, given that the module is part of a larger, definite-dimensional vector space and the underlying algebra is a semisimple Lie algebra or a matrix algebra over a field.

We provide an enhanced condition for biharmonic hypersurfaces to be minimal within Euclidean space, expanding on earlier studies that relied on conformal recurrence operators. Our novel condition, derived through conformal recurrence operators, serves as a more substantial foundation for biharmonic hypersurfaces to be minimal within Euclidean space, compared to the condition involving curvature operators identified in our previous research.

We establish fresh definitions for distances in rational $d$-dimensional space, along with various regular expression operations, and prove that these match the previously established results for one-dimensional space, except for a minor discrepancy in one case. Additionally, we develop new proofs for previous outcomes regarding finite automata recognition of subsets with rational point coordinates, along with a novel characterization of subsets with rational point coordinates that are reachable through a given set of transformation rules, and a new description of subsets with rational point coordinates that are directly specifiable using context-free regular expressions.

Theoretical frameworks such as CLN and BGL, used to study rare $B$ meson decays, assume a power-law relationship between decay rates to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant operators. However, recent studies have shown that a linear relationship may not always be accurate, and machine learning models can be used to describe the connection between rates more precisely. Using such a model, we calculate the contributions of dimension-six operators to rare decays, updating previous CLN tables with new results from 2-loop anomalous dimensions and existing 1-loop results. We find that some operators produce similar decay rates, allowing for consolidation into a single, representative operator, whereas others remain distinct due to significantly different scale evolution behaviors. Reorganized lists of operators with similar rate patterns can be found in the appendix.

A dynamical system is considered stable in a given state if small initial perturbations result in minor changes to the system's behavior. One method for evaluating stability involves examining how perturbations grow or decay over time, with a key indicator being the Lyapunov exponent. If a Lyapunov exponent is positive, then the distance between two systems will increase, indicating instability in the more complex system. Conversely, if an exponent is negative, further investigation is necessary to determine stability, as the central system may exhibit stable behavior or grow exponentially in specific directions. A novel perspective on stability is presented, focusing on the connection between Lyapunov exponents and area-expanding linear transformations. This analysis reveals that a system with multiple interacting oscillators will exhibit stable behavior if linearized expansions result in fractional loss of area in the relevant dimension(s). A simple harmonic oscillator serves as a model system for illustration purposes.

This research expands the concept of an angle function in hyperbolic spaces to local doubling spaces, addressing problems related to conformal embeddability. The research solves two specific problems: determining areas enclosed by curves with respect to an angle function, and demonstrating the ability to embed local doubling spaces within a hyperbolic space of a specified type. The method involves deriving basic properties of an angle function in local doubling spaces, as well as a more general version of Kigami's theorem.

Our research introduces the TPC (Transform-Preserving Construction) framework, which enables the generation of point cloud models that resist twisting transformations up to a certain order. This framework extends existing methods to construct models that are resilient against twisting transformations of order one. Additionally, we have developed new algorithms to construct models that are resistant against twisting transformations of order two for 3D point clouds and order three for 2D line clouds. Our research provides certified accuracy guarantees for these newly developed algorithms.

The integration of programming concepts and language specifics is highly complex, as seen in general-purpose programming languages like C.  AffectJ is a testing framework designed to aid programmers in identifying and fixing errors found in their code.  This framework consists of two primary components: a compiler-based analyzer that detects potential sources of common issues, and a testing environment that employs automated testing to verify these issues.  AffectJ's compiler adds metadata to code, enabling the tester to recompile code that has already been written, reducing the learning curve for programmers.  By providing both automated testing and analysis, AffectJ aims to streamline the process of writing tests and fixing errors, thus facilitating the education of programming concepts to beginners.  This work builds upon our previous research, "Designing Tests and Fixing Bugs for Programming Concepts," and is targeted towards instructors who teach programming fundamentals.  AffectJ's documentation includes multiple examples and guidelines for creating custom affectible concepts, as well as a repository of existing affectible concepts on the AffectJ website.  The source code of AffectJ is available on GitHub.  In the context of the general-purpose programming language C, we have developed affectible concepts for pointers, structures, and function pointers, which have been successfully utilized in courses at our institution.  The effectiveness of AffectJ was evaluated through a user study involving 120 undergraduate students from three different universities, which demonstrated a significant improvement in both learning programming concepts and writing efficient code when using the

We establish an equivalence between G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles and a specific subset of reduced p-adic Galois representations arising from crystalline extensions, without relying on complicated construction methods. This subset comprises all representations with p-power free trace and is synonymous with the subset identified by Fontaine and Matieu through an indirect approach.

A proposed method utilizing a genetic algorithm to optimize neural networks for self-sensing composites has been developed and tested. This technique aims to enhance the accuracy of damage detection in composites by fine-tuning the neural network's ability to analyze sensor data. The material used in this study was carbon nanotube reinforced polymer composites, which are capable of sensing damage through changes in electrical resistance. A impact test was employed to induce various levels of damage on the composite samples. The genetic algorithm was found to significantly improve the neural network's performance in distinguishing between damaged and undamaged states of the composites. The results showed that the optimized neural network demonstrated better detection capabilities than traditional machine learning models. Furthermore, a deeper analysis revealed that the genetic algorithm's optimization contributed to the neural network's ability to detect subtle changes in resistance data that correlate with damage levels.

We derive several integral identities involving generalized hypergeometric functions, which serve as a foundation for developing a systematic approach to proving these identities using geometric vector techniques, specifically by differentiating the fundamental representation of the harmonic analytic vector.

For groups acting on trees and a specific subgraph that results in a free product, we demonstrate how to identify a subgraph within which the group acts freely, assuming the subgraph is distinct from the entire graph and connects components that are not adjacent to the entire graph.

This research develops the Fundamental Inception Theorem to demonstrate a direct connection between the inception depth of a nested structure and the convergence rate of the Nested Neumann algorithm. A concise, general formula is also derived to calculate the minimum inception depth based on the given nested structure. A series of examples is provided to illustrate the applicability of this theorem and its resulting formula.

In contextual linear bandits, it's assumed that context dimensions are known in advance. This paper investigates a scenario where context distribution's characteristics are unknown but relevant to a decision-making process. It presents two new algorithms that trade off between action's communication and context's description. The first, "Optimal Algorithm 1", achieves the best possible regret when the action's distribution is known. When this information is unknown, "Optimal Algorithm 2" provides the best possible regret by combining a sample and a partition of the context space.

A comprehensive theoretical study has been conducted to investigate how polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and very small grains (VSGs) influence cooling behavior in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. To accomplish this goal, multiple physical processes are considered, including desorption, vibrational deexcitation, and gas-grain interaction. A detailed model is employed to examine the cooling curves of these disks, taking into account various grain sizes and temperatures. A critical finding is that the presence of VSGs allows for additional cooling through phosphine molecule formation. Furthermore, by analyzing observed emission spectra of disks, such as HH30 and GM Aur, it is possible to determine if PAHs or VSGs are responsible for cooling in specific areas of a disk. A notable discovery is that large grains or ice particles might be necessary for cooling in certain regions of a disk, especially in areas close to the disk's surface.

This research focuses on certain types of manifold structures, specifically graduate-shrinking Ricci solitons, and examines how harmonic functions that grow slowly will have a limited number of dimensions. A key aspect of this study involves deriving an upper bound on the dimensions of harmonic functions that satisfy a specific growth condition, as well as a fundamental inequality related to the volume growth of these functions. A generalized version of a previously known result concerning linear growth can be found in an appendix.

Neural networks are susceptible to embedded backdoors that allow triggering specific actions with compromised models. Although research has successfully implemented trigger-based backdoors in various tasks, it remains unclear how to dynamically alter backdoor behavior in response to changing conditions. Furthermore, existing methods struggle to accurately classify normal input data during backdoor activation. In contrast, our proposed technique, called D动作 (Dynamic Action), enables dynamic backdoor attacks on classification tasks with minimal training data required for the trigger class. Our D动作 (Dynamic Action)  activates backdoor behavior based on context, as demonstrated by three practical applications: classification, multi-task learning, and the MNIST dataset.

This paper introduces a new random walk based algorithm for learning from distributed data, where agents take turns choosing between updating their model and communicating with neighbors. The random walk approach helps agents reach more informative neighbors, which can mitigate communication inefficiencies. The paper proves the algorithm achieves the best known guarantees for both single-carrier and multi-carrier networks, and demonstrates its performance through experimental results.

A novel, adaptive mixing approach has been developed for semi-supervised medical image segmentation, addressing the challenge of combining labeled and unlabeled data. This method, called Consistent Mixed Regularization, incorporates a new term in the optimization process that regularly corrects mixed segmentations to reduce errors and inconsistencies. This term uses information from previous iterations to achieve consistent, usable combinations of data. To train the network, a combination of the mixed regularization and the adversarial loss is employed, and an innovative way of updating the adversarial loss has been discovered to account for the variable quality of mixed segmentations. Experimental results on publicly available datasets (ACR and LIDC) demonstrate the effectiveness of this Consistent Mixed Regularization strategy in terms of segmentation accuracy and speed compared to other established methods.

Quantum systems' nonlocal properties, such as entanglement, can be affected by measurement outcomes, leading to situations where certain properties are determined by measurements performed on remotely located particles. In multi-partite quantum systems, entanglement's complex nature means that specific particles might not contribute significantly to nonlocal effects and steering. A recent study has shown that even in fully entangled systems, a single particle may not exhibit noticeable nonlocality and influence other particles unless they are measured. In such cases, the determining factor is not the system's initial state but rather the outcome of the measurement performed on the particle in question. A specific example has been explored, where a single particle's entanglement could lead to nonlocality and steering in a trio of particles even when the system is in a product state, provided a certain measurement outcome occurs. In this scenario, the entanglement's source is not the particle's initial state but rather the entanglement generated through measurement on a trio of particles, which can be thought of as a "entanglement pump'.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and sensitive data from Internet of Vehicles (IoV) systems has been met with concerns from researchers and policymakers due to data security and privacy issues. This paper proposes a smart consensus mechanism called TCC, which is layered on a Blockchain network to address these concerns and promote trustworthy AI decision-making in IoV systems. The TCC mechanism incorporates a novel Credit Block Model to govern data storage and a Turbo Code-based encryption protocol to ensure privacy and security of vehicle data. Furthermore, it includes a sophisticated validation process to prevent malicious behavior and ensure the authenticity of data. Theoretical analyses along with simulation experiments have been conducted to evaluate the proposed mechanism, indicating significant improvements in data privacy, security, and trustworthy AI functionality in IoV systems. The findings suggest that the TCC mechanism can significantly reduce data risks and promote the utilization of valuable information in IoV systems.

High-throughput deep learning hardware is increasingly relevant due to AI applications. A new design, FDHT-LSTM, which represents an LSTM layer using a Fast Discrete Hartley Transform, has been proposed and a corresponding hardware accelerator, called TIEr, has been implemented. When compared to a typical LSTM module, the FDHT-LSTM module exhibits improved throughput and reduced energy consumption. In addition, TIEr outperforms regular hardware for LSTM layers in terms of throughput and is more energy-efficient. A TIEr-based LSTM hardware was found to process images using a ConvLSTMP block, achieving the highest known throughput of 10^7 images per second on small images and demonstrating considerable energy efficiency on large images.

Recently, a significant breakthrough occurred in the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, specifically for functions on algebraic curves over finite fields. This breakthrough involved a result stating that any polynomial with finite support in the Galois group of the function field's algebraic closure is actually part of a larger group with a known description. This description involves a product of symmetric groups, similarly structured to how the integral weight modular forms are classified in the theory of automorphic forms.

This research develops two novel proofs to establish the blow-up criterion for solutions of the Schrödinger equation in a bounded domain, partially surrounded by a boundary, under specific initial and boundary conditions. A linear Schrödinger equation is used as the model, and the proofs focus on proving the same blow-up outcome for solutions of the equation and their gradients, in the presence of a boundary. A previously established relationship between the energy of solutions and the $L^2$ norm of initial data is expanded upon, demonstrating an equivalent characterization of the condition involving the $L^2$ norm of initial data. Furthermore, this characterization leads to an alternative proof of a previously established blow-up criterion in a whole space setting. A previously established blow-up criterion in a half-line setting is also generalized to prove the blow-up outcome for solutions and their gradients in the presence of a boundary. A previously established relationship between the energy of solutions and the $L^2$ norm of initial data is expanded upon, demonstrating an equivalent characterization of the condition involving the $L^2$ norm of initial data.

A commutative algebra A is defined as having positive characteristic if its center Z is non-trivial, and as characteristic zero if Z is trivial. A key decomposition in commutative algebra theory involves the trace ideal, the center, and the algebra itself, denoted as Ide(tr_A), Z, and A respectively. Based on this decomposition, various modules over A can be analyzed, including derivations, their kernels, and their discrete structure. A notable category in this context is the category of (p,-q)-central modules, which consists of modules where which consists of modules where the kernel of derivation d has an explicit form. As a result, modules within this category share similar properties, and a comparison with modules in the category of Char-zero algebras can be made. Furthermore, algebras with a free center are found to have a more extensive discrete structure compared to algebras with a non-free center. Moreover, a characterization of (p,-q)-central modules in the context of Serre's theorem is provided, along with an exploration into the impact of characteristic on commutative algebra theory, particularly concerning the trace ideal, the center, and the underlying algebra.

In the realm of artificial intelligence, selecting among competing hypotheses based on their performance is a common problem. A key aspect of this process is ranking hypotheses, which can be done using utility functions that evaluate the impact of each hypothesis's mistakes on the overall outcome. This research develops a novel framework for deriving utility functions in various contexts, along with two general formulas that can be applied across all scenarios. A demonstration of this utility's practical value in machine learning is provided by showing how it can be used to prioritize hypotheses and make informed decisions.

This study introduces DiscSense, a multi-domain semantic relation dataset comprising English discourses with annotated markers and relations. Unlike existing datasets that focus on single relations or contexts, DiscSense explores various relations and contexts, making it an ideal evaluation tool for analyzing the impact of discourse markers on semantic relations. Furthermore, we present MultTaskBT, a multi-task learning model that can task multiple relations simultaneously, demonstrating its effectiveness on the DiscSense dataset by achieving the best results in three relation categories: cause-effect, contrast, and permit-prohibit relations.

We provide a generalization of the Jordanian twist, subsequently developing a simple, composition-rule form. This simplified version serves as a foundation for multiple generalized twists, closing the algebraic structure required for applying quantum algebra techniques in physics models.

We develop a modified Brzozowski's operator for regular expressions that serves as a foundation for a decision procedure to determine if one regular expression is contained within another. Our optimized Brzozowski's operator consists of multiple components, incorporates the empty set, and utilizes complementation. We also engineer a Brzozowski's operator for regular expressions over an extended character set that includes union and complement. Our Brzozowski's operator-based approach to determining containment takes the same time complexity as converting Brzozowski's automata to Thompson-Nielson form, which is exponential in the size of the regular expression for union and complement, but only until the set is empty, which incurs linear complexity in the size of the regular expression for settling on the empty set.

We provide a detailed explanation for conserved current OPE blocks in CFT$_{2}$, utilizing both AdS$_{3}$ and AdS$_{2}$ geodesic diagrams. By applying a dimensional reduction from AdS$_{3}$ to AdS$_{2}$, we observe various transformations in OPE blocks, specifically for the free scalar field. Additionally, we derive the reduced AdS$_{2}$ picture for a general conserved current, without relying on dimensional reduction. A key finding is that conserved current OPE blocks in CFT$_{2}$, utilizing AdS$_{2}$ geodesic diagrams, inherit the same representation structure as those utilizing AdS$_{3}$ geodesic diagrams. Moreover, we identify a new perspective on the AdS$_{2}$ CFT$_{2}$ gravity side, utilizing the AdS$_{3}$ picture, which allows for a more comprehensive understanding of massive gravity and its interactions.

A novel image processing technique is introduced, utilizing a lobster-eye optics system, that leverages the rotation of cross-like images to distinguish between near and far-field segments. This method enables the segmentation of the optical system into multiple areas based on the azimuthal angle of the pattern, allowing for wide-field-of-view, astigmatic optical systems to be divided into various sections with unique detection capabilities. A simulation using a Rayleigh scattering model demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique in distinguishing between near and far-field segments under varying conditions. Furthermore, a gas laser-based experiment confirms the technique's applicability in real-world scenarios, demonstrating its potential for use in large lobster-eye optics systems.

To improve the efficiency of hydrodynamic cosmological simulations, a fundamental challenge lies in accurately modeling halo collapse and subsequent structure formation, particularly for a scenario with an enhanced amplitude of initial scalar perturbations. Beyond simple overrelaxation techniques, we investigate a novel method based on a linear perturbation theory model, specifically a density-only version of Eulerian fluid dynamics, which is derived from the linearized Poisson equation. By adjusting this model to match the true evolution of a given system, we can overcome its linear limitations and apply it in a form of an external force in a hydrodynamic simulation. Using this density-only model in a context of a cosmological N-body simulation showed a significant reduction in the formation time of halos and improved agreement with a full linear perturbation theory analysis. Furthermore, by combining the model with an established halo finder, we observed a substantial enhancement in the formation of halos below a mass threshold of $10^{10}M_{\odot}$ and a significant improvement in the accuracy of halo mass predictions in a box size of $100Mpc$ and a resolution of $5kpc$.

The local detection of magnetic fields through atomic interferometry, as demonstrated in a recent experiment, has been found to be highly sensitive to even minor magnetic fluctuations.  A local magnetic field's impact on atomic motion is exploited in atomic interferometry, allowing for its detection at extremely low levels of noise.  In a gas-based atomic interferometer, a sensitivity of 10^-18 Tesla^-1 sqrt(Hz) has been achieved for certain frequency ranges, surpassing the fundamental limit set by quantum measurement uncertainty.  This achievement has resulted in the discovery of a stellar magnetic field with a strength of 2e-18 Tesla through a supernova remnant's detection.  A comparison has been made between the noise sensitivity of atomic interferometry and other precision measurement techniques, including optical interferometry and gravitational wave detectors.  A perspective has been offered on the potential applications of atomic interferometry in various areas, including planetary magnetic field detection, subatomic particle detection, and the study of neutrino properties.  Furthermore, a roadmap has been outlined for improving the sensitivity of atomic interferometry to atomic mass changes, which could lead to discoveries in fields such as astrophysics and particle physics.

Theoretical models often rely on assumptions about the relationship between magnetic adatoms or dimers and the local electron density at the surface of an s-wave superconductor. However, recent studies have shown that anisotropic magnets can exhibit behavior not captured by these models, specifically with regard to the spin-orbit coupling's impact on the placement of YSR state peaks. Based on an anisotropic magnetic model and considering the spin-orbit coupling's influence, we have developed a more comprehensive description of YSR states. This description accounts for the anisotropy-induced splitting of magnetic moments and subsequent formation of paired local moments in an anisotropic magnet. Using this description, we have recalulated the energy spectrum of YSR states in the presence of an anisotropic magnetic monopole and found that the usual pairing picture is not applicable due to the spin-orbit coupling's effect. Instead, we observed the formation of a single local moment in the magnetic dimer, leading to a zero-energy peak's disappearance and the emergence of a higher bound state. As the magnetic moment increases, the half-gap state reappears, and the bound state shifts closer to the Fermi level.

Deep convolutional neural networks have been highly successful in image classification tasks due to their ability to learn complex features from visual data. However, their reliability can be compromised when presenting unknown images, which is a significant limitation in practical applications. In an effort to boost the stability and accuracy of deep image classifiers, this research proposes a novel ensemble classification system called TIE-DCNN. By combining multiple, slightly different convolutional neural networks with different weight decay regulators, TIE-DCNN is designed to generate a diverse set of classifiers that can cope with various patterns in images. Furthermore, an efficient voting mechanism is introduced to determine the classification outcomes based on the ensemble's consensus. Experiments using three large image classification datasets - ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR-10 - demonstrate that TIE-DCNN significantly enhances the classification accuracy of deep neural networks across various scenarios, including normal, adversarial, and low-quality images. Notably, TIE-DCNN achieves the best results to date in the adversarial attack classification dataset benchmark - Robust Adversarial Attacks and Tests - without the need for expensive gradient descent computations.

The structure functions for W and Z bosons in proton collisions are examined, focusing on universal corrections from gluon splitting and jet function evolution. A framework is developed to calculate these effects, utilizing an operator product expansion similar to that in heavy quarkonia decay theory. The resulting power counting is utilized to categorize universal corrections as either mass-dependent or universal, with the universal category further subdivided into leading and next-to-leading logarithmic terms. A set of integral equations is derived to calculate the structure functions' evolution with energy, with examples provided for zero-transverse-momentum operators and those with non-zero transverse momentum. The underlying assumptions are validated by ensuring the new equations' consistency with existing knowledge on hadron structure functions.

We provide a new proof for a notable theorem in mathematical logic, which states that a formal system cannot prove the statement "if a statement is undecidable, then its negation is not decidable." Additionally, we present an enhanced version of this theorem, which concerns a situation where an unprovable statement within a formal system may still be decidable through an alternative logical approach.

This research focuses on linear fractional dynamic systems and examines conditions for linear subspaces to remain within those subspaces when subjected to a dynamic system. A key aspect of this study involves defining a new concept called "fractional dynamic subspace" that mirrors the behavior of linear subspaces in conventional dynamic systems but now in the context of linear fractional dynamic systems. A crucial result shows that if two linear subspaces meet certain criteria, the system can be designed such that the subspace is invariant to the dynamic process. Furthermore, this research develops a method for determining the largest invariant subspace of a given linear fraction dynamic system, as well as identifying the smallest number of dimensions required for a specified set of subspaces.

A novel regularizing strategy is introduced and proven for the solution of a parameter identification problem in a linear parabolic PDE.  This strategy involves derivative operators in the PNE (Polymer-Chen-Lai-Nirenberg) sense and is based on a new Carleman estimate that is specifically tailored for this problem.  A global observability inequality is a key component of this estimate and is obtained for the first time in the PDE at hand.  The resulting regularizer is highly efficient, can be numerically computed, and serves as the foundation for developing a nonlinear regularization theory for this inverse problem.  This includes a unique solution formula, an a-priori stability estimate, and an optimal regularization parameter choice rule.  Furthermore, the regularizer meets the minimal requirements for applying the Lipschitz source condition, enabling the development of an abstract framework that leads to the derivation of a semiglobal convergence rate bound and a global convergence rate bound under additional smoothness assumptions on the data.  Theoretical results are complemented by numerical experiments that illustrate the practicality of this approach.  The method is applied to a model parameter identification problem in heat conduction, demonstrating its utility in real-world scenarios.  An existing regularity result is generalised, showing that a global observability inequality can be obtained under the same assumptions with which the Carleman estimate was derived.  The existing regularity result is then applied to derive a global convergence rate bound in an appropriate function space.

We develop a new perspective on a dark matter model, dark parity, particularly in a context where a minimal dark sector interacts with the standard model through a dark axial vector force. This force is responsible for mediating dark matter interactions and gives rise to new heavy quarks that contribute significantly to vacuum polarization. To maintain vacuum stability and consistency with dark parity symmetry, we extend the standard model with an additional Higgs doublet. Utilizing a seesaw framework, we generate small dark parity breaking masses for the heavy quarks. Furthermore, we modify the standard model Higgs boson decay patterns and determine the parameter ranges through vacuum stability analysis. Additionally, we calculate the dark matter relic density and determine the connection between the new Higgs doublet and the standard model Higgs boson.
